title: Teaching
text:
Teaching is one of the most rewarding parts of my job. There’s something deeply satisfying about watching a student go from “I don’t understand R” to confidently analysing their own data, or seeing a field course spark someone’s passion for ecology.
I believe in learning by doing, whether that means getting your hands dirty in the field or wrestling with real datasets in R. Theory matters, but it sticks better when you’ve experienced the messiness of actual ecological data.

title: Biodiversity Forecasting
text: Climate change is reshuffling species distributions worldwide. To respond effectively, we need to anticipate these changes, but our predictions are only as good as our models. We work on making species distribution models more reliable by building in ecological realism.

title: Biodiversity Forecasting
text:
The Limitation of Correlative Models
Most species distribution models work by correlating where species occur with environmental conditions, then projecting to future climates. This works reasonably well for some purposes, but it misses crucial dynamics: Can the species actually disperse to newly suitable areas? Will populations persist through bad years? How do interactions with other species constrain distributions?

title: Biodiversity Forecasting
text:
Process-Based Approaches
We are interested in models that incorporate these processes explicitly. This means combining species distribution models with population dynamics, dispersal kernels, and mechanistic constraints. The models become more complex, but also more honest about what drives species distributions.
A concrete example: standard models might predict that a species “should” occur in northern Europe by 2050. But if that species only disperses 10 km per generation and there’s 500 km of unsuitable habitat in between, it’s not getting there. Process-based models can capture this.

title: Biodiversity Forecasting
text:
Data Integration
Good models need good data. We work on integrating different data sources (standardised monitoring surveys, citizen science observations, ringing recoveries) to improve both the spatial coverage and the temporal dynamics we can capture. Each data type has biases, but combining them thoughtfully can give us a more complete picture.

title: Animal movement and dispersal
text: Animal movement connects individuals to their environment across scales: from daily foraging decisions to seasonal migrations across continents. Understanding these movements is central to ecology and conservation, because they determine how populations are connected, how species track changing environments, and how individuals find resources and mates.

title: Animal movement and dispersal
text:
Dispersal: the missing piece
Dispersal (the movement of individuals from their birthplace to where they breed) drives almost everything in ecology. It determines gene flow, shapes range boundaries, allows colonisation of new areas, and rescues declining populations. Yet for most species, we simply don’t know how far individuals disperse.
Traditional approaches to studying dispersal face a fundamental challenge: you need to track individuals from birth to breeding, which is logistically impossible at large scales. Radio-tracking gives detailed data but for tiny sample sizes. Genetic methods tell you about long-term patterns but miss the ecological timescales we care about.

title: Animal movement and dispersal
section: Estimating dispersal from bird ringing data
text:
Estimating dispersal from bird ringing data
We work with bird ringing data: millions of records from decades of systematic marking across Europe. The challenge is that these data weren’t designed to study dispersal; they’re full of biases (ringers cluster near cities, recoveries depend on human density, etc.).
Together with collaborators, we developed Bayesian methods that account for these biases and extract reliable dispersal estimates. This produced the first standardised dispersal kernels for over 200 European bird species (Fandos et al. 2023, JAE).

title: Animal movement and dispersal
text:
What we have found
The big surprise from this work? Long-distance dispersal is far more common than we thought. Even “sedentary” species occasionally move hundreds of kilometres. This matters because these rare long-distance events are exactly what drive range expansions and maintain connectivity between distant populations.
We are now exploring why dispersal varies so much within species. The same species can show very different dispersal patterns depending on population density, habitat quality, or individual condition. Understanding this context-dependence is crucial for predicting how species will respond to environmental change.

title: RIMed-Fauna
text: Mediterranean rivers are defined by extremes. Winter floods reshape channels; summer droughts leave only disconnected pools, or nothing at all. This hydrological variability creates unique challenges for wildlife, and climate change is making these extremes more intense.

title: RIMed-Fauna
text: Mediterranean rivers are defined by extremes. Winter floods reshape channels; summer droughts leave only disconnected pools, or nothing at all. This hydrological variability creates unique challenges for wildlife, and climate change is making these extremes more intense.

title: RIMed-Fauna
text:
The Project
RIMed-Fauna investigates how terrestrial vertebrates (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians) adapt to the temporal dynamics of Mediterranean river systems. We’re working in Spanish National Parks to understand:

Which species depend on river corridors and how?
Where are critical refugia during drought?
How will predicted changes in river flow affect wildlife communities?

title: RIMed-Fauna
text:
My Role
I contribute species distribution modelling expertise and supervise Claudia Mediavilla’s MSc research within the project. We’re building models that integrate hydrological variability with wildlife occurrence data, a methodological challenge because most SDM approaches assume static environments.
We’re also deploying camera traps to monitor wildlife use of riparian habitats across seasons.

title: Landscape structure shapes dispersal kernels within species: new paper in Oikos
text:
Together with Jette Wolff, Cécile Albert, Greta Bocedi, Justin Travis and Damaris Zurell, we have published a new study in Oikos on how landscape structure shapes dispersal within species.
Using individual-based simulations of movement for four animal species across landscapes that differ in habitat amount and fragmentation, the study derives emergent dispersal kernels and compares five probability density functions. Fat-tailed (log-normal) kernels consistently describe dispersal best, and habitat fragmentation strongly reshapes the kernels by altering movement trajectories. Habitat amount has a weaker and less consistent effect.
The practical message for modellers: a kernel estimated in one landscape does not transfer cleanly to another. This is exactly the kind of context-dependence that INTRADISP is trying to quantify with empirical ringing data.
Wolff, J., Fandos, G., Albert, C. H., Bocedi, G., Travis, J. M. J., & Zurell, D. (2026). Habitat fragmentation and amount drive within-species variation in dispersal kernels and limit transferability across landscapes. Oikos. doi:10.1002/oik.12209 · Code on Zenodo

title: Simple traits beat complex syndromes at predicting bird dispersal: new paper in Communications Biology
text:
Our paper with Rob Robinson (BTO) and Damaris Zurell (Potsdam) is out in Communications Biology.
Dispersal syndromes, the idea that suites of correlated traits describe how species disperse, are popular but rarely tested against empirical dispersal data at scale. Using the most comprehensive dispersal dataset available for European birds, we asked how dispersal syndromes form and how well they predict dispersal across species.
The answer is that single mechanistic traits do better than composite syndromes. Body mass and life history dominate median dispersal distances, whereas flight efficiency shapes the rare long-distance movements that matter most for range expansion and connectivity.
Fandos, G., Robinson, R. A., & Zurell, D. (2026). Simple mechanistic traits outperform complex syndromes in predicting avian dispersal distances. Communications Biology, 9, 376. doi:10.1038/s42003-026-09676-x · Code and data on Zenodo

title: INTRADISP
text:
When we talk about “how far species X disperses,” we’re glossing over enormous variation. Within any species, some individuals stay close to home while others travel hundreds of kilometres. This isn’t random noise; it reflects individual condition, local density, habitat quality, and other factors we’re only beginning to understand.
This variation matters. If we want to predict how species will respond to climate change, we can’t just use average dispersal distances. A population might expand rapidly or barely move at all, depending on which individuals are dispersing and under what conditions.

title: INTRADISP
text:
What We’re Doing
INTRADISP uses the EURING ring-recovery database to quantify intraspecific dispersal variation across European bird species. We’re asking:

How much does dispersal vary within species compared to between species?
What environmental and individual factors predict this variation?
Can we build dispersal models that account for context-dependence?

title: SHAREPOINT
text: Understory birds in tropical rainforests often forage in mixed-species flocks, with stable social relationships that persist over years. Does this social organisation shape how parasites move through the community? SHAREPOINT combines field data on bird social networks with parasite screening to test whether who you associate with predicts what you carry.

text: Understory birds in tropical rainforests often forage in mixed-species flocks, with stable social relationships that persist over years. Does this social organisation shape how parasites move through the community? SHAREPOINT combines field data on bird social networks with parasite screening to test whether who you associate with predicts what you carry.

title: SHAREPOINT
text:
What we’re doing
Field-based research in French Guiana, combining mist-netting, individual marking and observation of flock membership with molecular screening of blood parasites. The analysis links social network structure to parasite sharing and transmission.

title: SHAREPOINT
text:
Our role
We contribute to the fieldwork and to the spatial and network analysis, building on previous experience with rainforest bird communities in French Guiana (CEBA projects).

title: Conservation Applications
text: We try to make our research useful beyond academia. This means working on questions that matter for conservation practice and collaborating with people who can actually implement the results.

title: Conservation Applications
text:
Large Carnivore Expansion
One line of work we are proud of focuses on large carnivores in Iberia. Wolves, bears, and lynx are expanding their ranges across Spain and Portugal, which is good news for conservation, but also a management challenge. Where will they go next? Which areas are critical for connectivity? Where are conflicts with humans most likely?
We supervised students who tackled these questions using species distribution models and landscape connectivity analysis. The results identify priority areas for proactive conservation: places where action now could facilitate successful recolonisation rather than scrambling to respond after conflicts emerge.

title: Conservation Applications
text:
Threatened Species Assessment
We have also worked on improving population assessments for data-deficient species. Traditional monitoring often suffers from “preferential sampling”, meaning we collect data where it’s convenient, not necessarily where it’s representative. We developed occupancy models that correct for this bias, applied to 22 years of Black Stork monitoring data in Spain.
The resulting population estimates were more robust than previous assessments and contributed to the species’ evaluation in the Spanish Red List.

title: Conservation Applications
text:
Current Applied Work
Currently, we are involved in projects on Mediterranean river ecosystems (RIMed-Fauna) and bat habitat modelling. These applied contracts keep us grounded in real conservation problems and remind us why the methodological work matters.

title: Field Technology
text: New technology is changing what we can observe in the field. Cheap cameras, acoustic recorders and satellite data let us monitor species that are hard to detect, at scales that were impossible a decade ago. We are building pipelines that turn these raw data streams into usable biodiversity information.

title: Field Technology
text:
Camera trapping
We deploy camera trap networks in Mediterranean ecosystems as part of the RIMed-Fauna project, monitoring how terrestrial vertebrates use riparian habitats across seasons. There is something exciting about checking SD cards and discovering what walked past while you weren’t there. The methodological challenge is to turn detection histories into robust occupancy and activity estimates in environments that change drastically between winter floods and summer drought.

title: Field Technology
text:
Bioacoustics
In collaboration with Raúl Bonal (UCM) we deploy AudioMoth recorders for passive acoustic monitoring. Acoustic data open up possibilities for species that are hard to detect visually, such as bats and nocturnal birds, and for continuous monitoring over long periods.

title: Field Technology
text:
Why it matters for modelling
Sensor data are not a substitute for good models; they are what makes better models possible. Camera traps and recorders produce standardised, repeatable detections that can be combined with citizen science and ringing data in the integrated models we develop in our monitoring and modelling work.

title: Research
text: Our research focuses on the ecological processes that drive the distribution and abundance of animal populations. We combine fieldwork, large-scale data synthesis (bird ringing, citizen science, camera traps) and quantitative modelling to tackle questions across spatial and temporal scales, and we try to make the results useful for conservation.

title: Research
text:
Approach
Our work typically combines big datasets and quantitative methods:

Ring-recovery data from EURING and national schemes, one of the largest individual-level animal movement datasets in the world
Citizen science observations, especially eBird
Bayesian hierarchical models implemented in R
Camera trapping and bioacoustic monitoring in the field

We are committed to open science. Code and data for our papers are available on GitHub and archived on Zenodo.
